sentences.text: They went through the box slowly, together, over the whole first morning.
Silvia let Kristjan open each envelope carefully.
Most of the letters inside were dull — bills, receipts, formal business correspondence from long-dead merchants.
Some were sad — messages of condolence that had never reached the family.
A few were sweet.
Silvia would read the old handwriting for Kristjan, translating the old formal Estonian into modern speech, sometimes laughing softly at a phrase.
About an hour in, she found one that made her stop.
It was a small folded letter in a thin brown envelope.
On the outside, in careful young handwriting: To Miss Marie Kask, of Räpina village, near Tartu.
Estonia.
The postmark was Tartu, December nineteenth, eighteen ninety-eight.
The letter had been returned twice — Silvia showed Kristjan the small stamps on the back.
Return, no such address.
Return, unknown recipient.
And then a small pencil note in some old postmaster's hand: Address vague.
Hold.
Silvia looked at it for a long moment.
She said, "Let us open this one."
Inside was a single sheet of thin brown paper.
The handwriting was young and neat and slightly leaning.
Silvia read it in Estonian first, softly, to herself, and then translated for Kristjan.
"My dearest Marie," she read.
"I have this morning finished the purchase of the little house in Räpina — the one behind the mill, with the two windows facing the river.
I will come for you at Christmas as we agreed.
Please do not worry about the roof.
It is a good roof and I have inspected it myself.
I am, in the meantime, thinking of three things I love about you and I will tell you which they are when I see you.
Yours, always, Aleksander Rebane." Silvia lowered the letter slowly.
"December nineteenth," she said.
"He never came for her at Christmas."
Kristjan asked, "Why not?" Silvia said, "I do not know.
But I can guess.
The winter of eighteen ninety-eight to ninety-nine was the worst influenza winter Estonia had seen in fifty years.
There is a note in one of the library annals that Tartu lost several hundred people between December and February.
He was very young.
Twenty-five, twenty-six, at most, from the handwriting.
If he died in that flu, this letter — sent just a few days before — would have arrived at the Räpina post office and found nobody with clear enough address, and been returned.
And her family may have known him only as 'Marie's young man from Tartu' — no fixed street, nothing formal.
That is why the address was vague.
It was written to a girl in a small village where everyone knew each other.
They did not need a street.
But once he was gone, and the letter came back to Tartu, nobody there knew what to do with it either.
So it came here.
And it has been here ever since."
Kristjan sat looking at the letter.
Then he said, "Aunt Silvia.
Kask is a very common Estonian name.
Marie Kask must have married someone else after Aleksander died.
She might have had children.
Those children might have had children.
Those grandchildren might be alive right now.
Some of them might live in Tartu.
We could find them."
Silvia looked at him.
She said, "That is exactly what I have been thinking for fifty years." She smiled a small sad smile.
"But I never did it, Kristjan.
I never once opened the genealogy books and tried.
I was always going to do it next month.
It is one of those things." She was quiet.
Then she said, "But you are here.
You have a bus back to Tartu in eleven days.
And Kask is, as you say, a common name in the Tartu region.
Perhaps we look.
If we find nothing, we put the letter back.
If we find someone — we shall see."
They went upstairs to the genealogy reading room.
Silvia knew it well.
She showed Kristjan how to use the parish record books — the old ones from Räpina were on microfiche, the newer ones digitized.
They looked for a Marie Kask, born around eighteen seventy-five to seventy-seven, who might have married someone in Räpina or nearby after eighteen ninety-eight.
It took them three afternoons, spread over four days.
They found her.
Marie Kask, born eighteen seventy-six in Räpina, married Jaan Tamm of Räpina in nineteen hundred and two — four years after Aleksander's letter.
They had five children.
The children had grown up, moved away, had their own children.

Silvia traced the youngest daughter's line — Anna Tamm, born nineteen fifteen — through a marriage to a Kask cousin (which was common in small villages), through two more generations, to a woman still alive in Tartu today, aged sixty-two, whose name was Piret Kask, and who taught music at a small school.
Silvia sat back in her chair when they had confirmed it.
She said, "She is the great-granddaughter of Marie Kask.
Marie was her great-grandmother, on her mother's side.
She almost certainly still lives at the address in the phone book.
And she is your neighbor, more or less.
Tartu is not big."
That evening in the apartment, they sat at the small table by the window.
The letter from Aleksander lay in the middle.
Silvia had written Piret Kask's address in her small notebook.
She was quiet for a long time.
She said, "I do not know how to do this, Kristjan.
It has been fifty years.
I have never delivered one.
I do not know what one is supposed to say."
Kristjan thought.
He said, "You just — go.
And you say, we found this.
We think it was meant for your great-grandmother.
And you give it to her.
And whatever she does, she does." Silvia smiled at him — a real full smile this time.
"That is very good advice from a ten-year-old," she said.
"That is exactly how we shall do it.
Tomorrow I telephone her.
If she agrees, on Friday, we take the bus to Tartu together.
You are on your way home anyway.
We deliver it, and then you go on to your mother."
